pages.x: After 11 September, President George W. Bush and the British prime minister, Tony Blair, argued that Saddam Hussein was hiding chemical and biological weapons and might give them to terrorists. UN inspectors searched and found none. Millions marched against war in cities around the world, but in March 2003 America and Britain invaded without the UN's approval.

The invasion began on 20 March 2003. As bombs and missiles lit up Baghdad, American and British armies raced north from Kuwait, and the British took Basra. Baghdad fell in three weeks. On 9 April a crowd, helped by American Marines with an armoured vehicle, pulled down a giant statue of Saddam.

On 1 May Bush declared the end of major combat, standing on an aircraft carrier beneath a banner that read Mission Accomplished. But there was no plan for what came next. The Americans disbanded Iraq's army and sacked members of Saddam's party, leaving hundreds of thousands of angry men without work. No weapons of mass destruction were ever found.

Saddam was found in December 2003, hiding in a hole in the ground near his home town of Tikrit. An Iraqi court sentenced him to death for the killing of 148 men from the town of Dujail, and he was hanged on 30 December 2006.

Insurgents, from Saddam's old officers to al-Qaeda in Iraq, fought the Americans with roadside bombs. In 2006 al-Qaeda blew up the golden-domed Shia shrine at Samarra, and Iraq slid into a civil war between Sunni and Shia. Photographs of prisoners abused by American guards at Abu Ghraib shocked the world.
pages.of: of Iraqis died; no count is agreed

pages.x: In 2007 Bush sent 30,000 more troops under General David Petraeus, and many Sunni tribes, sick of al-Qaeda's brutality, turned against it. The killing fell sharply. Iraqis voted in elections, and in December 2011 the last American troops left. Nearly 4,500 of them had died.

The war ended the rule of a dictator who had killed hundreds of thousands of his own people, and Iraqis now vote for their leaders. But the weapons it was fought over did not exist, and its chaos gave birth to the Islamic State, which in 2014 seized Mosul and a third of Iraq. It also made Iran far more powerful in the region.
